sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: When Philip II was murdered in 336 BCE, Diodorus says, several Greek states moved against Macedonian control, and the Thebans voted to drive out the garrison Philip had placed in their citadel, the Cadmea. In the spring of 335 Alexander campaigned against the Thracians, the Triballians and the Illyrians. While he was away, exiles slipped back into Thebes by night, killed two officers of the garrison outside the Cadmea and persuaded the assembly to revolt, insisting that Alexander had been killed in Illyria; Lendering names the Athenian orator Demosthenes as the source of that rumour.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: Arrian says Alexander took the revolt seriously because he already suspected Athens, and feared that Sparta, the Aetolians and doubtful states in the Peloponnese would join Thebes. Diodorus describes the help Thebes sought and did not get: Demosthenes sent weapons, Athens voted support but sent no army, and the Peloponnesians who came as far as the Isthmus waited to see how the war would go. The new king had not yet crossed to Asia, and a Greek revolt behind him would have put the expedition at risk.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: In Arrian, Alexander camped close to the Cadmea to support its garrison and still preferred terms to battle. Plutarch says he asked only for the surrender of two leaders, Phoenix and Prothytes, and offered an amnesty to anyone who came over. Diodorus says he would gladly have granted the Thebans peace and alliance, to be free for the war with Persia, but that once he saw they despised him he decided to destroy the city and so take the heart out of anyone else who might rise against him.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: Thebes lay in Boeotia, with the Macedonian garrison in the citadel of the Cadmea. The Thebans had cut it off with a double stockade, in Arrian's account, or with deep trenches and heavy stockades in Diodorus's. Alexander came from the north-west through Eordaea and Elimiotis to Pelina in Thessaly and into Boeotia by Onchestus, then moved round to the gate on the road to Eleutherae and Attica. Arrian's narrative of the fighting runs from the stockade by a hollow way to the temple of Heracles, through the gates, to the temple of Amphion and the market-place.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Alexander had the Macedonian army that Philip had trained, with Greek allies; Arrian names Phocians, Plataeans and other Boeotians among them, and Diodorus Thespians, Plataeans and Orchomenians. The garrison in the Cadmea, commanded according to Diodorus by Philotas, strengthened its walls and stocked missiles. The Thebans had their citizens, cavalry and light infantry; Diodorus says they put freed slaves, refugees and resident aliens on the walls and fought in front of the city themselves. The revolt was led by the returned exiles, some of them Boeotarchs, who Arrian says expected no mercy. The sources' figures are not repeated here.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: Alexander first camped by the precinct of Iolaus to give the Thebans time to send envoys; instead their cavalry and light infantry attacked his outposts and were driven back. The next day he moved round to the gate on the road to Eleutherae and Attica and camped near the Cadmea. Arrian places the brigade of Perdiccas in the advanced guard, close to the Theban stockade, with that of Amyntas son of Andromenes beside it. Diodorus describes a set-piece arrangement after three days of preparation: one division against the palisades, one facing the Theban battle line and one in reserve.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: In Arrian's account, which follows Ptolemy, Perdiccas broke into the stockade without waiting for the signal and Amyntas followed. Alexander sent in the archers and the Agrianians and brought up the rest of the army so that the two brigades would not be cut off. Perdiccas was badly wounded at the second stockade. His men drove the Thebans back as far as the temple of Heracles, where the Thebans turned and routed them, killing Eurybotas, the captain of the archers, with many of his men. Alexander then advanced with the phalanx in order against the Thebans, whose ranks had broken in pursuit, and drove them back through the gates before they could be shut.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Alexander's choices were to march south at once, to wait outside the city rather than assault it, and, once fighting began, to commit his whole force behind Perdiccas. The Thebans' leaders chose to fight: Diodorus says they voted for it unanimously, and Plutarch that they answered Alexander's demand with a counter-demand for Philotas and Antipater and a call to all who would free Greece. Diodorus has Alexander answer a proclamation calling him the tyrant of Greece by vowing the extremity of punishment.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: In Arrian the Macedonians followed the fugitives through the gates, and the walls, empty because the defenders were out in front of them, fell with them. Some joined the garrison of the Cadmea; others ran along the walls into the market-place, and when the Thebans at the temple of Amphion saw themselves attacked from several sides, their cavalry broke out into the plain and the infantry scattered. Diodorus has a different sequence: Alexander committed his reserve, saw a postern gate left unguarded and sent Perdiccas through it, and the garrison burst out of the Cadmea into the confused Thebans. Plutarch, too, has the garrison fall on their rear.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: Arrian says the Thebans were then killed less by the Macedonians than by the Phocians, Plataeans and other Boeotians, who took revenge for old injuries, in the houses and in the temples, sparing neither women nor children. Alexander left the settlement to the allies who had fought with him. They voted to garrison the Cadmea, raze the city, divide its territory and sell the women, the children and the surviving men into slavery, except priests and priestesses, the guest-friends of Philip and Alexander and those who had acted for the Macedonians. It is said, Arrian adds, that Alexander spared the house and descendants of the poet Pindar. Diodorus and Plutarch give figures for the dead and the enslaved that are not repeated here.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: The effect was immediate. Arrian says the Arcadians, who had set out to help Thebes, condemned those who had urged them to; the Eleans recalled exiles friendly to Alexander; the Aetolians sent envoys asking pardon; and the Athenians abandoned the Great Mysteries, brought their property into the city and sent envoys to congratulate him. He demanded the surrender of Demosthenes, Lycurgus and other leaders, then relented, either from respect for Athens or because he was eager to cross to Asia; only Charidemus was exiled, and went to Darius. The allies also voted to rebuild Orchomenus and Plataea. Lendering says the League of Corinth ratified Alexander's acts.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: Thebes shows terror used as a policy. The destruction of one city settled Greece behind Alexander within days, without further fighting, and freed him to cross to Asia. Handing the sentence to Thebes's neighbours made it the act of the Greek alliance, and also let old local hatreds decide the fate of its people. Plutarch says the memory later gave Alexander remorse.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: Who began the assault is disputed. Arrian, following Ptolemy, has Perdiccas attack without orders and Alexander follow to save him; Diodorus has Alexander prepare an assault for three days and send Perdiccas through a postern gate himself. Who decided the city's fate is told differently too: Arrian gives the decision to the allies, Diodorus to the common council of the Greeks, and Plutarch says Alexander destroyed Thebes to terrify the Greeks and to satisfy the complaints of the Phocians and Plataeans. Arrian puts much of the killing on the Boeotian neighbours. Accounts written from Alexander's side had reasons to spread the responsibility.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: Arrian gives the fullest military narrative and the aftermath in Greece, from Ptolemy, who served in the campaign. Diodorus, from the vulgate tradition, gives the Theban preparations, the appeals to other states and a different account of the assault. Plutarch gives the exchange of demands and Alexander's motives and later remorse. Lendering's survey places the revolt between the northern campaign and the crossing to Asia.

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: Persian support for Perinthus against Philip II in 340 BCE made war between Macedon and Persia, in Livius's words, inevitable. Philip's advance force under Parmenion and Attalus was already in Asia when he was assassinated in 336. Alexander joined it with the main army in 334.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: Darius III had only recently come to power after the murder of Artaxerxes IV and had revolts to deal with elsewhere, so no royal army met the invasion. The defence of western Asia Minor fell to the regional satraps, with local levies and Greek mercenaries.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Alexander needed an early victory to secure his foothold and open the road south. Diodorus says Memnon of Rhodes urged the Persian commanders to avoid battle, strip the countryside and carry the war into Europe, and that they rejected the plan as beneath their dignity. Livius judges the river position they chose instead a clever one, since it forced Alexander to turn west rather than march south with his communications exposed.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: The Granicus, the modern Biga Çayı in north-western Türkiye, is a small river. In Arrian, Parmenion warns that parts of it were deep and its banks high and in places abrupt. Livius states that the banks are too steep for horses to climb and that the landscape has changed little since antiquity.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Alexander commanded the right wing with the Companion cavalry; Parmenion commanded the left, with the Thessalian and allied Greek cavalry, and the phalanx battalions held the centre. Persian command was shared among satraps and nobles, among them Arsites, Spithridates and Mithridates, Darius's son-in-law, with Memnon and his sons among the cavalry. Arrian gives round figures for the Persian cavalry and mercenaries; Livius gives none.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: In Arrian the Persians stretched their cavalry along the bank, massing it opposite Alexander, who was conspicuous by his armour, and kept the Greek mercenary infantry behind on higher ground. Diodorus also places the cavalry in front and the infantry behind. Livius reads this order as a defence against a crossing.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: Arrian has Alexander reject Parmenion's advice to camp and cross at dawn. An advance guard under Amyntas, with Socrates's squadron, entered the river first; Alexander then led the right wing across at an angle to the current so that his line would emerge facing the enemy. Plutarch also places the attack late in the day, but Diodorus has the army cross at dawn before the Persians could stop it.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Arrian presents Alexander's refusal to wait as a matter of reputation: an army that had crossed the Hellespont should not be halted by a stream, and delay would encourage the enemy. The satraps' rejection of Memnon's advice had already committed them to a battle that a strategy of avoidance might have denied Alexander.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The first Macedonians to land took heavy losses under missiles and cavalry attack. Alexander's charge then turned the struggle on the bank into a close mêlée. His spear broke; he unhorsed Mithridates and killed Rhoesaces, and Cleitus cut off the arm of Spithridates as he struck at the king from behind. Arrian credits the Macedonians' strength, experience and cornel-wood lances. The Persian centre broke first, then both wings.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: The Persian cavalry fled without a long pursuit. Alexander then surrounded the Greek mercenaries, who had stayed where they stood; Plutarch says they asked for terms and were refused. Most were killed. Arrian says the prisoners were sent in chains to labour in Macedonia for fighting against Greeks, and that Arsites fled and killed himself.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: The road south lay open: Sardis and Ephesus fell without a fight, and Dascylium and Gordium were left unprotected. Alexander sent captured armour to Athens as an offering from himself and the Greeks, the Spartans excepted. Persian sea power remained, and Alexander met no further resistance until the Persian fleet appeared at Miletus.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: A defensive position depends on how its arms work together: cavalry posted on a bank to stop a crossing cannot be supported by infantry held far behind it. Speed and personal example exploited a divided command, but at a personal risk that nearly ended the campaign in its first battle.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: Arrian and Plutarch describe a direct assault late in the day; Diodorus describes a crossing at dawn before the Persians could react. Livius prefers Diodorus, arguing that horses could not have climbed the banks and that the Persian order of battle implies Alexander had already crossed safely. The accounts also disagree on who struck whom in the mêlée, and their army and casualty figures are not repeated here. Plutarch attributes the massacre of the mercenaries to anger rather than judgement.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: The study compares three ancient narratives: Arrian's, Diodorus's and Plutarch's, who cites Aristobulus for the Macedonian dead. Livius's article sets these traditions against the ground and against the Persian order of battle Arrian reports.

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: After the Granicus and the capture of Miletus in 334 BCE, Alexander disbanded his fleet: Arrian says it was short of money and no match for the Persian one, and that he meant to defeat the Persian navy from the land by taking the coastal cities it needed. Diodorus says the bulk of the Persians and mercenaries, with the most enterprising commanders, then gathered at Halicarnassus, the largest city of Caria. Darius made Memnon of Rhodes commander in the west; Diodorus adds that Memnon sent his wife and children to the king, to keep them safe and to win his trust.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: Lendering argues that Memnon's aim was to win time. While he held Halicarnassus the Macedonians could not safely go east, Darius could raise a new army, and with the Persian fleet at sea Memnon could take the garrison off whenever he chose. Briant counts the long resistance at Halicarnassus among the signs that Persian defeat in battle did not bring a quick collapse of the empire. Caria's ruling family was divided: Ada, daughter of Hecatomnus, had been driven from power by Pixodarus, after whose death the Persian king sent Orontobates to rule Caria, and she met Alexander on his march, offered him her fortress of Alinda and adopted him as her son.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Alexander needed the city to carry out the strategy he had chosen when he gave up his fleet: to deny the Persian navy its harbours. Memnon needed only to hold out for as long as the siege served Darius. Lendering judges that Alexander must have understood that he would lose whatever the outcome: he could take the city only at heavy cost, while the defenders could leave before their losses grew too great.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: Arrian says the city's position was naturally strong and that Memnon had made good whatever it lacked; Lendering adds that the walls were recently built and designed against siege engines. A deep ditch ran in front of the walls. Arrian names a gate toward Mylasa, the side of the city toward Myndus, a citadel facing Mylasa, a triple gate, and two strongholds that held out after the city fell: one on the island called Arconnesus and another called Salmacis. Triremes in the harbour supported the defence.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Memnon held the city with many Greek mercenaries and Persian troops, alongside Orontobates, the Persian ruler of Caria; Diodorus names two Athenian exiles, Ephialtes and Thrasybulus, among the commanders. Alexander brought the shield-bearing guards, the Companion cavalry, the infantry brigades of Amyntas, Perdiccas and Meleager, the archers and the Agrianians; Diodorus says his siege engines and supplies came by sea. The sources' figures for losses are not repeated here.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: Alexander camped close to the city, Arrian says, as if he expected a long siege. On the first day a sortie at the Mylasa gate was driven back. A few days later he took a strong force round to the Myndus side, both to inspect the walls and to take Myndus, whose people had offered to surrender by night. No one opened the gates; he had brought no engines or ladders, a tower his men undermined fell without opening a breach, and reinforcements arrived from Halicarnassus by sea, so he returned to the siege.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: The Macedonians filled the ditch and brought up siege towers. A night sortie to burn them was beaten off. Then two drunken soldiers of Perdiccas's brigade attacked the wall alone; the fighting that followed nearly carried the city, because two towers and the wall between them were already down. The defenders built a crescent-shaped brick wall behind the breach, and when Alexander brought his engines against it, they sallied again and burned part of a shed and of a tower. A few days later came the largest sortie, through the breach and through the triple gate at once.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Memnon's choices were active defence, with repeated sorties against the engines and a new wall behind each breach, and in the end evacuation. Alexander's were to try Myndus, to press the siege with engines, and, at the moment the city seemed about to fall, to call his army back. Arrian says he did so to see whether the Halicarnassians would offer to surrender, because he still wished to save their city. After it fell he chose not to besiege the strongholds, judging them of little use to the defenders now that he held the city.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The great sortie failed. At the breach the defenders were driven back by men round Alexander and by stones from the engines; at the triple gate a bridge over the ditch broke under the fleeing crowd, and the gates were shut too early in a panic, leaving many outside. Diodorus describes the same crisis as a sortie led by Ephialtes that drove the Macedonians back under fire from a tall wooden tower until older veterans, exempt from the fighting, closed ranks and killed him. Orontobates and Memnon then decided they could not hold out, fired their own siege tower, the magazines and the houses near the wall, and withdrew.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: Alexander entered the burning city that night and killed those still setting fires, but ordered that Halicarnassians found in their houses be spared. Arrian says he razed the city, left the strongholds under watch with a garrison under Ptolemy, and made Ada ruler of all Caria. In Diodorus, Memnon left his best men in the citadel with supplies and shipped the rest of the army and the stores to Cos, and Alexander walled the citadel off with a wall and trench.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: Before winter Alexander sent the newly married Macedonians home from Caria and marched along the coast into Lycia and Pamphylia to take its harbours. Lendering says that Alexander and his generals must now have decided to go on to Phoenicia, so that no enemy fleet could again enter the Aegean. The Persian fleet was still at sea: Diodorus says Memnon took Chios and the cities of Lesbos and alarmed Euboea, until he fell ill and died.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: A defender who controls the sea can treat a city as something to be spent for time. Memnon gave up Halicarnassus only when holding it no longer paid, and took much of his force away by sea. Alexander won the city and lost months, which is why the next step was to take the Persian fleet's bases one by one along the coast.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: Lendering says the ancient sources present the siege as a victory, but that Alexander must have known better, and notes that after one failed attack he had to ask for a truce to recover his dead, something he never did again. Diodorus records that request and says Memnon granted it against the advice of Ephialtes and Thrasybulus; Arrian does not mention it. The accounts of the evacuation differ: Arrian sends the defenders to the island and to Salmacis, Diodorus to the citadel and to Cos. Arrian has Neoptolemus, a Macedonian deserter, die fighting for the Persians in a sortie, while Diodorus has an officer of that name die among the Macedonians at the gates.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: Arrian gives the fullest account of the siege, from Ptolemy, who served in it. Diodorus gives the Persian command, the truce and the sortie of Ephialtes. Lendering's survey sets out Memnon's strategy of delay and doubts the ancient verdict of victory. Briant's article in the Encyclopaedia Iranica places Halicarnassus in the Persian resistance that followed the Granicus.

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: After the Granicus the only organized Persian resistance in the west was the fleet under Memnon and Pharnabazus, largely made up of Phoenician ships. In autumn 333 BCE Alexander entered Cilicia through the Cilician Gate, aiming at the Phoenician ports.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: Darius III raised a large royal army, recalling Greek mercenaries from the Aegean, and marched from Babylonia into Syria. Livius reconstructs his plan as defeating Alexander on the plains of Cilicia or northern Syria and then using the fleet to cut off his retreat.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Arrian has the Macedonian exile Amyntas urge Darius to stay on the broad plain near Sochi, where his numbers and cavalry would count. Darius, reading Alexander's delays in Cilicia as reluctance to fight, crossed the Amanus by the Amanian Gate instead and came down behind him at Issus, where his troops killed the sick Macedonians left there.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: The armies met on the narrow coastal strip between the Amanus mountains and the Gulf of Issus, at the river Pinarus south of Issus, which Livius identifies with the modern Payas. Only the beach suited cavalry, and rain had made the banks slippery. Callisthenes, as reported by Polybius, put the width of the plain at about fourteen stades.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Darius took the centre, as Persian kings customarily did, with Greek mercenaries facing the phalanx and kardakes on either side. Alexander led the Companions on the right; Parmenion commanded the left by the sea, ordered not to lose contact with it so that the army could not be outflanked. The ancient totals for Darius's army are not credible, and Polybius showed that even Callisthenes's figures could not fit the ground.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: Darius sent cavalry and light infantry across the river to screen his deployment, then recalled them and massed most of his horse on his right by the sea. Troops on the foothills on his left overlapped Alexander's right. Alexander moved the Thessalians behind the phalanx to his left unseen, strengthened his right with two Companion squadrons, and drove the troops on the hill back with Agrianians and archers.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: Alexander confirmed that Darius was behind him by sending a ship along the coast, recrossed the pass by night and unfolded the column into line as the plain widened. Livius dates the battle to 5 or 6 November 333 BCE, from a Babylonian record of an eclipse and the marching time; Arrian gives the Athenian month Maimacterion. The Macedonians advanced slowly until they were within missile range; then Alexander charged across the river on the right.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Darius chose to leave the open plain for the narrow coast, and then to fight on the defensive behind the river, building stockades where the banks were easiest to climb; Arrian reads this as a loss of nerve. Alexander chose to turn back and attack at once rather than let Darius hold his line of communications.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The Persian left broke as soon as Alexander's charge reached it. In the centre the phalanx, disordered by the riverbed, opened a gap that Darius's Greek mercenaries attacked hard, and Ptolemy son of Seleucus fell there. On the seaward wing Persian cavalry under Nabarzanes pressed the Thessalians and allied Greek horse back toward the river. Alexander's victorious right then wheeled against the mercenaries' flank.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: Darius fled, first in his chariot and then on horseback, leaving his shield, mantle and bow; the Persian cavalry broke once it learned of his flight, and many were trampled in the narrow roads. Alexander pursued until dark. The camp fell with Darius's mother, wife and children, and Parmenion was sent to seize the treasure and baggage at Damascus.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: Phoenicia and Egypt were left largely unprotected, with Tyre and Gaza the main exceptions. Darius wrote offering alliance and a ransom for his family; Alexander replied with grievances and demanded recognition as king of Asia. Darius raised a new army, which Alexander met at Gaugamela less than two years later.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: Narrow ground can cancel a numerical advantage, and a commander who leaves open country for a cramped field gives up his main asset. Where authority is concentrated in one person, an attack aimed at his position can decide the battle. Livius calls Issus Alexander's personal triumph, the point after which he rather than Parmenion clearly directed the war.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: The identification of the Pinarus is not certain. Polybius criticized Callisthenes's account because its numbers and frontages could not fit the ground. Arrian has Darius flee as soon as his left broke; Diodorus describes fighting around his chariot and a change to a second chariot, which Livius reads as a sign that he did not mean to abandon the battle. Livius's detailed reconstruction rests partly on his own estimates of timing and archery.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: Arrian's narrative is compared with Diodorus and with Polybius's critique of Callisthenes. Arrian credits Ptolemy son of Lagus, who rode with Alexander, for the story that the pursuers crossed a ravine filled with bodies. Livius's three-part reconstruction also draws on Curtius Rufus.

sources.title: The siege of Tyre (332 BCE), with Curtius Rufus 4.4.10–21 (trans. J. Yardley)
Arrian, Anabasis of Alexander 2.15–24 (trans. E. J. Chinnock)
Diodorus Siculus, Library of History 17.40–46 (Loeb translation)

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: After Issus Alexander did not pursue Darius but moved down the Levantine coast. Byblos and Sidon submitted, and Tyrian envoys met him on the march to say that their city would do whatever he commanded.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: The Persian fleet still controlled the Aegean and the Hellespont, threatening Alexander's communications, and its crews came largely from the Phoenician cities. Taking those cities would deprive the fleet of its bases and its men.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Arrian gives Alexander a speech arguing that Egypt and Babylon could not safely be attempted while Persia held the sea, and that taking Tyre would bring the Phoenician fleet and Cyprus over to him. Livius regards the siege as strategically unnecessary and its cause as religious: Tyre refused Alexander the right to sacrifice to its god Melqart, whom the Greeks identified with Heracles, and Arrian has the Tyrians refuse to admit any Persian or Macedonian into the city. Diodorus gives the Tyrians' own reasons: to keep faith with Darius and earn his gratitude, to tie Alexander down in a long siege while the king prepared, and confidence in their island, their forces and help from their colonists at Carthage. He has Alexander resolve to take any risk rather than let the army be held in contempt by a single city.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: Tyre stood on an island, walled high on every side. Arrian says the strait was shallow and muddy near the mainland and about three fathoms deep beside the city. The city had two harbours, one facing north toward Sidon and one facing south toward Egypt.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Alexander had his field army and engineers, but at first too few ships; Arrian says Tyre still had the advantage at sea. The Tyrian king Azemilcus was away with the Persian fleet. Later, Phoenician and Cypriot squadrons and engineers joined Alexander.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: Alexander began a mole from the mainland, built of stone and timber with stakes driven into the mud. Near the city the workers came under missile fire from the walls and attack from Tyrian triremes, so two towers carrying engines, hung with hides against fire, were raised on the mole.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: Livius dates the siege from January to July 332 BCE. A Tyrian fireship burned the first towers, and Alexander widened the mole and went to Sidon for ships. Diodorus adds that as the mole advanced the Tyrians sent part of their women and children to Carthage, that a gale wrecked part of the mole and Alexander rebuilt it with whole trees to break the waves, and that the defenders' engineers met each attack with new devices: spinning wheels to deflect missiles, padded hides to absorb stones, barbed tridents and nets to drag men from the siege bridges, and heated sand poured on the attackers. Plutarch records that during the siege Alexander led a raid against the Arabs of the Antilibanus. With the Phoenician and Cypriot squadrons Alexander blockaded both harbours, cleared stones dropped in the approaches and brought ship-mounted engines against the walls. Arrian dates the fall to the Athenian month Hecatombaeon.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Alexander's decisive choice was to accept that the city could not be taken from the land alone and to assemble a fleet. Diodorus says that after one assault was beaten back his first impulse was to abandon the siege and march to Egypt, and that he changed his mind because it would be a disgrace to leave the Tyrians the glory, with only Amyntas son of Andromenes supporting him. The Tyrians chose to defend the city rather than admit a Macedonian presence, a choice Arrian presents as caution while the outcome of the war was still uncertain.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The ships of Aradus, Byblos and Sidon left the Persian fleet when their cities submitted, and the kings of Cyprus followed, giving Alexander command of the sea. The Tyrians declined battle and blocked their harbour mouths, and a midday sortie against the Cypriot ships was beaten back. Engines on ships then broke the wall facing Egypt.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: Hypaspists under Admetus and Coenus's battalion crossed from ships into the breach while the fleets forced both harbours; resistance ended at the shrine of Agenor. Plutarch says Alexander ordered the last day of the month to be counted as an earlier date so that his seer's prediction of capture within the month could still come true, and that the assault grew so fierce that troops left in camp ran to join it. Diodorus has Alexander cross to the wall by a bridge from a siege tower while a ram breached it elsewhere, and the Tyrians fight on behind barricades in the streets. Arrian says the Macedonians were enraged by the length of the siege and by the Tyrians' killing of captured Macedonians on the walls. Those who had taken refuge in the temple of Heracles, including King Azemilcus and Carthaginian envoys, were spared. The rest were killed or sold into slavery, and both Curtius and Diodorus report crucifixions.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: The Tyrians had recalled their ships from the Aegean, as had the other Phoenician cities, ending the Persian naval offensive there; with Tyre fallen, the fleet had lost its Phoenician bases. Alexander sacrificed to Heracles in the city, and Diodorus says he installed a new king. The road south to Gaza and Egypt was open. Briant cites the seven-month siege as evidence that the Persian empire did not collapse after Issus: the coastal advance to Egypt was far from easy.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: A navy can be defeated from the land by taking its ports, yet an island fortress could not be taken without ships. Engineering persistence mattered, and so did politics: the naval strength that decided the siege came from cities whose allegiance had changed.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: The motive for the siege is debated: Arrian presents a strategic argument, Livius stresses the refusal of the sacrifice, and Diodorus stresses Tyrian loyalty to Darius and hope of Carthaginian help. Diodorus and Plutarch fill the siege with omens: a sea monster stranded against the mole, Apollo's statue bound to its base so that the god could not desert to Alexander, and in Plutarch a dream of a satyr read as “Tyre is thine”. Diodorus kills Admetus in an earlier, failed assault; Arrian has him die leading the final one. Arrian, Curtius and Diodorus give different figures for those killed, crucified and enslaved, and they are not repeated here. Curtius reports that Sidonians serving with Alexander secretly carried many Tyrians to safety, which Arrian does not mention. Diodorus judges that Tyre endured the siege bravely rather than wisely.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: Arrian gives the fullest narrative of the engineering and naval operations. Livius presents Curtius Rufus's account of the final assault and the reprisals, noting that Curtius drew on earlier Greek writers, and sets the siege in the wider Levantine campaign. Diodorus, in the Loeb translation on LacusCurtius, belongs to the same dramatising tradition as Curtius but alone gives the Tyrians' reasons for resisting and their counter-measures. Plutarch adds the omens and the last day of the siege; Pierre Briant's article in the Encyclopaedia Iranica places Tyre in the history of Persian resistance.

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: After Tyre fell, most of Palestinian Syria had submitted. Batis, the eunuch governing Gaza, refused; he had hired Arab mercenaries and laid in food for a long siege, confident that the city could not be stormed.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: Gaza stood at the edge of the desert on the road from Phoenicia to Egypt. Darius meanwhile offered terms that Alexander rejected, and prepared for further war; Livius says Batis's resistance bought the king time to raise a new army. Diodorus describes Persian resistance elsewhere at the same time: Agis of Sparta, with Persian ships and money, won over most of Crete, and Persian officers who had escaped from Issus held cities for Darius or raised troops. Briant argues that this resistance has been underestimated: the advance from Issus to Egypt was far from easy.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Arrian says Alexander's engineers judged the wall impossible to take by force, and that he insisted because a success would alarm his enemies while a failure would discredit him before the Greeks and Darius. Prestige and the security of the road to Egypt both weighed in the decision.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: Arrian places Gaza about twenty stades from the sea, across heavy sand, on a high mound surrounded by a strong wall. Livius describes a town on a steep hill with strong walls.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Batis held the city with a garrison that included Arab mercenaries. Alexander had his field army, and the siege engines used at Tyre were brought up by sea.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: Alexander had a mound raised against the walls so that his engines could reach them, built highest against the southern wall, where an assault seemed easiest.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: During a sacrifice a bird dropped a stone on Alexander's head, which the seer Aristander read as a sign that the city would fall but that the king must take care that day. Plutarch tells the omen differently: a clod dropped by a bird struck Alexander's shoulder and the bird was caught in the cords of a siege engine. Fighting to relieve hard-pressed troops during a sortie, Alexander was struck in the shoulder by a catapult bolt that passed through his shield and breastplate. The mound was then extended round the city, miners undermined the walls, and the fourth assault succeeded.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Alexander's decision to besiege at all, against his engineers' judgement, is the central choice. Batis chose to resist rather than submit when the rest of the region had already done so.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: Mining brought down sections of the wall. At the fourth assault the phalanx attacked from all sides, through the breaches and with ladders; Neoptolemus was first over the wall, and the gates were opened from within.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: The defenders fought on inside the city and were killed at their posts, and the women and children were sold into slavery. Curtius says Batis was brought to Alexander alive and that Alexander, in a rage, had him dragged round the city behind a chariot while still breathing, in imitation of Achilles.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: Alexander resettled Gaza with people from the surrounding area and used it as a fortress. The coastal road to Egypt, his next objective, was open. Plutarch says he sent quantities of the spoils home to his mother, his sister and his friends, including frankincense and myrrh for his old tutor Leonidas.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: A modest fortress on strong ground could impose a long siege, and a commander's concern for reputation could justify an operation that strategy alone might not. The killing and enslavement that followed show what resistance could cost a besieged population.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: The length and date of the siege differ: one Livius page gives about four months and a fall in October 332 BCE, while the page on Curtius dates the capture to November; Diodorus gives two months and Briant several weeks. The treatment of Batis comes from Curtius; Arrian's narrative does not mention his fate, nor do Diodorus and Plutarch. Arrian and Plutarch tell the omen of the bird differently. Arrian's dimensions for the mound are not repeated here.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: Arrian supplies the narrative of the siege, Curtius, in Livius's translation, the death of Batis, and Livius's survey the place of the siege in the Levantine campaign. Diodorus, who mentions the siege in a single sentence, and Plutarch, who gives the omen and the wound, are read in the Loeb translations on LacusCurtius; Pierre Briant's article in the Encyclopaedia Iranica sets Gaza among the Persian commanders who kept resisting after Issus.

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: After his earlier victories over Persian armies, Alexander moved from the Mediterranean coast into Mesopotamia in 331 BCE. Darius III had meanwhile assembled a new army drawn from across his empire, each contingent under its own commander.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: Alexander lingered in Tyre and other cities while Greek affairs, including the rising of Agis III of Sparta, demanded attention. Darius made a further peace offer, which Alexander rejected. Diodorus says it offered all the land west of the Euphrates, a large sum of silver and the hand of one of Darius's daughters; Parmenion advised acceptance, and Alexander answered that the world could no more have two kings than two suns. Reinforcements Alexander expected from Europe never arrived, possibly because Antipater needed them against Agis.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Darius sought a battle on open ground where his numbers, cavalry and scythed chariots could be used, having been persuaded that the narrow field at Issus had cost him. Diodorus adds that he had longer swords and lances made, believing Alexander's men had held the advantage in weapons at Issus, and drilled his troops daily for fear that so many peoples of different speech would fall into confusion. Badian has Mazaeus shadow Alexander's march and perhaps steer him toward the ground Darius had chosen. Alexander needed to defeat the king's army in the field to make good his claim to rule Asia.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: The armies met on a broad plain near Gaugamela, north-west of Arbela (modern Erbil); Plutarch insists the battle was fought at Gaugamela, not Arbela as most writers said, and explains the name as “camel's house”. Arrian reports that the Persians had long before levelled the uneven ground so that chariots and cavalry could move freely. The exact site cannot be fixed with certainty; Badian thinks the sources point to the area east of Mosul, south of the Jabal Maqlub.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: The Persian army combined many regional contingents, Greek mercenaries, a few Indian elephants and scythed chariots. Arrian's reported Persian totals are not credible counts, and Livius gives no totals. Alexander commanded the Companion cavalry on the right; Parmenion commanded the left wing.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: Darius stood in the centre with his kinsmen and guard. Bactrian and Scythian cavalry under Bessus, with chariots in front, faced Alexander's right, while Greek mercenaries faced the phalanx. Alexander placed a second line behind the first, with orders to face about if the army were surrounded, and set angled flank guards on both wings.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: The Macedonians crossed the Tigris largely unopposed in mid-September, and a lunar eclipse followed on about 20 September. Diodorus says Mazaeus had been sent to hold the ford but thought the river too deep and fast to cross and went to burn the countryside instead, and that the Macedonians crossed chest-deep with locked arms; Badian holds that Mazaeus's orders were not to oppose the crossings at all. On 30 September, Badian writes, Alexander reconnoitred within sight of the Persians, keeping them alert by day and awake by night; Plutarch has Darius review his army by torchlight while Alexander sacrificed with his seer. The Persian army spent the night before the battle under arms. On 1 October Alexander edged to the right, a cavalry fight developed on that flank, the chariots were neutralized, and Alexander then charged the Persian centre.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Arrian reports that Alexander rejected Parmenion's advice to attack at night, citing the risks of night fighting in unfamiliar country. Plutarch gives the refusal a political reason: a defeat in daylight would leave Darius no excuse, as he had blamed mountains, defiles and the sea before. Diodorus and Plutarch both say Alexander slept so late that his officers issued the first orders on their own authority; in Diodorus it was Parmenion. Diodorus says the phalanx was told to clash spears on shields to panic the chariot horses and to open lanes for any that came on. Darius, fearing a surprise attack, kept his army standing in formation overnight. During the battle Darius sent cavalry around the Macedonian right to halt Alexander's movement.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: As Persian cavalry was drawn into the fight on Alexander's right, a gap opened in the Persian front. Alexander formed a wedge of Companions and nearby infantry and drove toward Darius. The opportunity arose from the Persians' own outflanking effort rather than from a fixed plan. Badian's reconstruction agrees: Darius sent his best cavalry to his left, the wedge went through the resulting gap and the phalanx attacked frontally, both making for the king.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: Darius fled and his army dispersed. Diodorus calls him a clever strategist who used the dust to escape in an unexpected direction; Badian says he was persuaded to flee to save his kingdom. Meanwhile Persian troops reached the Macedonian camp. Diodorus says Mazaeus sent horsemen round the flank and that captives joined them, though Darius's mother refused to go; Badian has Persian and Indian troops break through gaps in the line and plunder the camp instead of turning on the Macedonian rear. Alexander turned back to help Parmenion's hard-pressed wing, then pursued to Arbela, where he took the royal treasure and Darius's chariot but not the king himself. The Babylonian diary records that the king's troops deserted him.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: The battle decided the fate of the Achaemenid empire. A contemporary Babylonian diary calls the victor “king of the world”, and Darius escaped to Media intending to raise another army. Badian adds that Mazaeus, who had led the Persian right, surrendered Babylon soon afterwards and was made its satrap, and that Alexander held Persepolis by January 330 BCE.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: Preparing ground for one arm can tie an army to that ground. Alexander's second line, ordered to face about if surrounded, shows how a reserve can protect against the breakthroughs a broad enemy line makes likely.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: Dust hid much of the fighting, so its exact course is unknown. Arrian says Darius fled first, while the contemporary diary says his troops abandoned him; Livius prefers the diary. Badian finds Arrian's account unsatisfactory and warns that Curtius and Diodorus, who follow the dramatising “vulgate”, are confused and cannot safely be used to fill its gaps; he calls the meeting of the two kings, in which Diodorus has Alexander's javelin kill Darius's driver, fictitious. Plutarch repeats a complaint, partly in the words of Alexander's court historian Callisthenes, that Parmenion fought sluggishly; Badian thinks it uncertain whether Parmenion's appeal ever reached Alexander. Greek accounts may also carry Macedonian propaganda, and Badian calls their troop figures worthless; none are used here.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: Arrian's narrative draws on earlier accounts, citing Aristobulus for the captured Persian order of battle. Livius sets the Greek tradition beside the Babylonian Astronomical Diaries, which date the eclipse and the battle independently. Diodorus and Plutarch, in the Loeb translations on LacusCurtius, give the vulgate and biographical traditions, with the peace offer, the crossing of the Tigris and the raid on the camp; Ernst Badian's article in the Encyclopaedia Iranica weighs them and reconstructs the battle from the Persian side.

phases.description: Parmenion's wing is pressed and the camp raided; Alexander returns, then pursues to Arbela.

perspectives.name: Alexander III of Macedon
perspectives.objective: Destroy Darius's new army in battle and with it the king's authority.
perspectives.known: Captured Persian riders reported that Darius was near. The Persians held a broad plain prepared for cavalry and chariots.
perspectives.uncertainty: The Persian line far overlapped his own, and he could not know whether his wings would hold against envelopment.
perspectives.constraints: Expected reinforcements from Europe had not arrived. In Arrian's account he judged a night attack too risky in country the enemy knew better.
perspectives.forces: The Macedonian phalanx, Companion cavalry, Thessalian and allied cavalry, and light troops such as Agrianians and archers.
perspectives.terrain: Open, levelled ground that favoured the larger Persian cavalry and the chariots.
perspectives.logistics: A fortified camp, with the baggage guarded by Thracian infantry; it was raided during the battle.
perspectives.decision: He refused a night attack, built a second line and angled flank guards, edged to the right and charged into the gap in the Persian front.
perspectives.outcome: Darius fled, but a call for help from Parmenion drew Alexander back, and the king escaped to Media.

perspectives.name: Darius III of Persia
perspectives.objective: Fight on open ground where numbers, cavalry and scythed chariots could be used, unlike the narrow field at Issus.
perspectives.known: Alexander had rejected his last offer of terms and crossed the Euphrates and Tigris, and was approaching the prepared battlefield.
perspectives.uncertainty: When and how Alexander would attack; Arrian says he feared a night assault.
perspectives.constraints: An army of many peoples under their own commanders, who in Diodorus's account spoke different languages; Livius describes their morale as shaken by the eclipse and other omens.
perspectives.forces: Regional cavalry from Bactria, Media, Parthia and elsewhere, Greek mercenaries, a few elephants and scythed chariots.
perspectives.terrain: A broad plain he had chosen and levelled for his chariots.
perspectives.logistics: His base at Arbela held treasure and royal property, which fell to Alexander after the battle.
perspectives.decision: He had new long weapons made and the plain levelled, kept his army under arms overnight, sent cavalry around Alexander's right, while Mazaeus sent horsemen against the Macedonian camp, and launched the chariots against the phalanx.
perspectives.outcome: When Alexander's charge reached his centre he fled, or in the Babylonian account was abandoned by his troops, and escaped east to Ecbatana.

sources.title: Arrian, Anabasis of Alexander 3.18 (trans. E. J. Chinnock)
Diodorus Siculus, Library of History 17.68 (Loeb translation)

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: After Gaugamela Alexander took Babylonia and Elam and wanted to reach Persis, the Persian homeland, before winter. The Royal Road linked Susa with Persepolis and Pasargadae. The army divided: Parmenion took the baggage and heavier troops along the road, while Alexander led the Macedonian infantry, the Companions and the light troops through the Zagros.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: Persepolis held a royal treasury. Ariobarzanes, satrap of Persis, an office Livius thinks Darius created during the war, set out to block the mountain route. Shahbazi identifies him as a son of the Persian noble Artabazus, raised in Persian and Greek culture and for some years at the Macedonian court, who had led Persian units at Gaugamela; after that defeat each province was left to defend itself. On the way the Uxians had been massacred, and Livius says no one else then dared to stand in Alexander's way.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Ariobarzanes needed to hold the pass, or at least delay Alexander, to protect Persepolis. Shahbazi says he chose a gorge because the Macedonian army was unbeatable on the plain, and the narrow ground would deny it formation, combined arms and numbers. Alexander needed speed: Arrian says he reached Persepolis before its guards could plunder the treasury.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: Livius places the Persian Gate in the Tang-e Meyran, a valley of the Zagros north-east of Yasuj that is wide at first and then narrows into a gorge, with Ariobarzanes's position near the village of Cheshmeh chenar. Shahbazi describes the road from Susa forking on the way into Persis: the main branch ran round by the south, while the shorter and harder track ran through narrow defiles, and it was on this track that Ariobarzanes made his stand. Diodorus and Curtius call the place the Susian Rocks or Gate. The passes were snowbound in winter. Rockfall and road building make the line of any wall hard to identify today.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Alexander had the Macedonian infantry, the Companion cavalry, light cavalry, Agrianians and archers. Ariobarzanes held the slopes and the pass; Livius cites Curtius for catapults among his weapons. Shahbazi calls the Greek figures for Persian infantry valueless and argues that Ariobarzanes could hardly have mustered more troops than he had led at Gaugamela, so that his force was much smaller than Alexander's column. Arrian's and Diodorus's figures are not repeated here.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: According to Arrian, Ariobarzanes built a wall across the pass and camped beside it. Shahbazi, following the explorer Aurel Stein, thinks it was probably a line of heaped stones with outworks in front and the camp behind. Livius describes troops on the northern slope ready to roll boulders, and archers and catapults on the southern slope.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: Livius dates the battle to about 20 January 330 BCE. The Macedonians entered the valley, apparently without effective reconnaissance, and were caught where it narrowed; Diodorus and Shahbazi both say the Persians let them advance some way before attacking, with boulders rolled and javelins thrown from the heights, and the front had to withdraw, leaving its dead. Diodorus says Alexander thought it shameful either to abandon the dead or to ask for them, since that would admit defeat. Alexander then marched by night along another route to the Persian rear, destroyed the outposts before daylight and attacked the camp at dawn, while Craterus attacked the wall on a trumpet signal.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Alexander divided his force. Craterus stayed at the camp with his own and Meleager's battalions, some archers and cavalry, under orders to attack the wall when trumpets sounded behind it. Alexander took the hypaspists, Perdiccas's battalion, the lightest archers, the Agrianians and part of the Companions on the mountain path. Arrian says Amyntas, Philotas and Coenus led the rest toward the plain to bridge the river on the road into Persis.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: Caught between Alexander's force and Craterus's attack, the Persians broke. Many were cut down inside the fortifications, which Arrian says Ptolemy had been posted to hold, and others fell over the precipices. Shahbazi quotes Curtius on the defenders fighting on even when disarmed, dragging their attackers down. Ariobarzanes escaped into the mountains with a few horsemen.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: Alexander crossed the bridged river and reached Persepolis before its treasury could be plundered, also taking the treasury at Pasargadae and appointing Phrasaortes satrap. Livius says the commander at Persepolis refused Ariobarzanes entry and that he was probably killed. Shahbazi sets out two traditions: Arrian's, in which he escaped to the hills, and Curtius's, in which he broke through toward Persepolis, was barred by its garrison and returned to fight to the end.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: Alexander burned the palace at Persepolis, about four months after his arrival according to Livius. Arrian reports that Parmenion argued against it and that Alexander called it revenge for the Persian destruction of Athens; Arrian judges the act unwise.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: Speed without reconnaissance led the army into an ambush. Recovery depended on local knowledge, a night march and a fixing force timed to attack at the same moment. A frontal attack on a prepared defile was costly; turning it was decisive.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: The site is disputed: Livius places it in the Tang-e Meyran, while Abuzar Hemati proposes a site between Kopan and Yasuj and a battle fought by local nomads, which Livius rejects; Shahbazi reports that the site is generally sought, following Stein, at the Tang-e Khas. Livius doubts the story of a guide because it resembles Herodotus's account of Ephialtes at Thermopylae, and doubts that a wall was needed. Arrian and Shahbazi have prisoners guide the march, while Diodorus names a single bilingual captive, a Lycian who had herded goats in the mountains; Shahbazi notes that ancient and modern writers alike saw the battle as a Persian Thermopylae. Arrian sends Philotas to bridge the river, while Livius has Philotas attack a Persian-held rock. Ariobarzanes's death is not securely documented, and Shahbazi rejects the Greek strength figures that modern historians have repeated.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: Arrian gives the clearest account of the divided forces and the signals. Livius's article, which updates an earlier study by Henry Speck, sets the narrative against the terrain and the Persepolis Fortification Tablets and draws on Curtius for the catapults. Diodorus, in the Loeb translation on LacusCurtius, gives the repulse, the guide and the night march through deep snow. A. Shapur Shahbazi's article in the Encyclopaedia Iranica tells the battle from the Persian commander's side and summarises Curtius's version of his end.

phases.title: Into the Zagros
phases.description: The army divides; Alexander takes the mountain route toward Persis while Parmenion follows the Royal Road.

phases.title: Ambush in the defile
phases.description: The Macedonians are caught where the valley narrows and withdraw, leaving their dead.

phases.title: Night march
phases.description: Alexander leads a picked force by another route; Craterus waits at the camp for the signal.

phases.title: Attack from two sides
phases.description: Outposts and camp fall, Craterus attacks the wall and Ariobarzanes escapes into the mountains.

perspectives.name: Alexander III of Macedon
perspectives.objective: Reach Persepolis and its treasury before they could be emptied or defended.
perspectives.known: The pass was held; his first attack had failed against troops on the heights.
perspectives.uncertainty: Whether the path described by prisoners would bring him to the Persian rear in time.
perspectives.constraints: Snow and ice, a narrow defile, and an army divided, with Parmenion's half on the road.
perspectives.forces: Macedonian infantry, the hypaspists, Companion cavalry, Agrianians and archers.
perspectives.terrain: A valley narrowing into a gorge, with slopes held by the defenders.
perspectives.logistics: A light force on a forced march, with the baggage sent along the Royal Road.
perspectives.decision: He left Craterus to fix the wall and led a night march round to attack from behind on a trumpet signal.
perspectives.outcome: The defenders broke and he reached Persepolis before its treasury was plundered.

perspectives.name: Ariobarzanes, satrap of Persis
perspectives.objective: Hold the Persian Gate to protect Persepolis.
perspectives.known: In Livius's reconstruction he knew the terrain and anticipated the Macedonian movements; Shahbazi says he judged the Macedonian army unbeatable on open ground.
perspectives.uncertainty: Whether his position could be turned by another route.
perspectives.constraints: He faced Alexander's striking force while Parmenion's column advanced along the Royal Road.
perspectives.forces: Troops on the slopes with stones, archers and, according to Curtius as cited by Livius, catapults; Shahbazi argues the force was far smaller than the Greek figures.
perspectives.terrain: A narrow gorge where defenders above could strike attackers below.
perspectives.logistics: A camp beside the wall in a snowbound pass.
perspectives.decision: He blocked the pass and let the Macedonians advance into the narrow ground before attacking from the heights.
perspectives.outcome: His position was turned. In Arrian he escaped to the hills; in Curtius, as Shahbazi reports, he was refused entry to Persepolis and died fighting, an end Livius also thinks probable.

sources.title: Arrian, Anabasis of Alexander 4.3–5 (trans. E. J. Chinnock)

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: Alexander treated the Jaxartes (Syr Darya) as the north-eastern frontier of his empire and in July 329 BCE founded Alexandria Eschate, the furthest Alexandria, at modern Khujand, as a garrison against the nomads north of the river. The foundation helped provoke a Sogdian revolt, and in the fighting Alexander was struck on the head and neck by a stone. Plutarch adds an arrow wound below the knee that splintered the bone, and says the blow to the neck clouded his sight for some time.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: As nomad horsemen, whom Arrian calls Scythians and Livius Sacae, gathered on the far bank, the Sogdian leader Spitamenes besieged the garrison at Maracanda to the south. Alexander sent a relief force under Pharnuches and turned on the nomads himself. Briant explains why the north mattered: the Bactrian and Sogdian nobles were fighting to keep their privileged position, and both Bessus and Spitamenes could count on long-standing alliances with the Saka chiefs beyond the Syr Darya.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Alexander wanted a decisive local defeat to secure the river line. Arrian says the nomads shot across the river and taunted him, and that he risked the crossing despite unfavourable sacrifices rather than be mocked as Darius I had been by the Scythians. Livius suggests the nomads expected to catch the Macedonians as they landed.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: Livius describes the river as wider than a bowshot, so that boats would come under arrow fire partway across; Arrian calls it narrow and names it the Tanais. The fighting took place on open ground on the far bank, near the new city.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Alexander had Companion and allied cavalry, horse-lancers, archers, slingers, Agrianians and other light troops, the phalanx and bolt-shooting engines. The nomads were mounted archers who relied on mobility. Livius notes that the steppe suited neither the phalanx nor the Companion cavalry against horse archers.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: Arrian says the army was drawn up at the river with hide floats prepared. On a signal the engines shot at horsemen riding along the far bank; one was struck through shield and breastplate and fell, and the rest drew back from the bank.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: Livius dates the battle to August 329 BCE. Archers and slingers crossed first and screened the landing until the cavalry was across. A first detachment of allied cavalry and horse-lancers was surrounded and harried by the horse archers. Alexander then attacked with light infantry mixed among his cavalry, and charged with Companion regiments, the horse-lancers and the rest of his horse.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Alexander chose to fight rather than simply hold the river line. Livius reads the forward detachment as bait that the nomads misjudged; Arrian describes it only as too weak to hold them. Alexander then combined light infantry with cavalry so that the horsemen could not wheel away.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: Once light infantry and cavalry attacked together, the nomads could no longer wheel and escape, and their flight began. Their commander Satraces was among the dead.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: The pursuit was cut short: Alexander drank bad water, fell seriously ill and was carried back to camp. Plutarch says that he pursued the routed Scythians a long way despite suffering from diarrhoea. Envoys of the Scythian king then came to say that the attack had been the work of raiders, not of their state, and Alexander sent a courteous reply. Livius adds that he released the prisoners without ransom. Plutarch cites a letter of Alexander to Antipater in which the Scythian king offered him his daughter in marriage.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: The victory did not end the revolt. Spitamenes destroyed the relief force sent toward Maracanda at the river Polytimetus. The war in Sogdiana continued into 327 BCE, with forts stormed, their men killed and women sold, and parts of the country ravaged. Livius says the northern frontier itself was not seriously threatened again. Briant counts three years of heavy fighting, in which Alexander changed his tactics and supply arrangements, used indiscriminate terror to force the nobles to submit, and settled Greek and Macedonian colonists in garrisons and new towns that ended the nobility's dominance.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: Against a mobile opponent, missile engines, light infantry and cavalry had to work together to force close combat. A tactical victory over one enemy could not settle a revolt behind the lines.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: The exact crossing site near Khujand is not fixed, Arrian calls the river the Tanais, and Plutarch says Alexander took it for the Tanais. Livius's account of the nomads' misjudgement is a modern reconstruction, as is his view that this was tactically Alexander's most brilliant victory. Arrian's casualty figures, and his belief that the whole enemy force would have been destroyed but for Alexander's illness, are not repeated as fact; Plutarch has the illness but not the interrupted pursuit. Plutarch records the story that the queen of the Amazons visited Alexander here, and the many writers, including Ptolemy and Aristobulus, who called it fiction. The envoys' claim that the attack was unofficial sits uneasily with Briant's long-standing alliances between the Sogdian leaders and the Saka chiefs; no account from the Saka side survives.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: Arrian supplies the narrative of the crossing and the fighting. Livius's article reconstructs the tactics, and his survey of the Sogdian campaigns places the battle in the wider revolt, warning that Arrian's account of these years is fragmented and hard to follow. Plutarch's Life of Alexander, in the Loeb translation on LacusCurtius, adds the wounds, the illness and Alexander's letter on the Scythian king's offer; Pierre Briant's article in the Encyclopaedia Iranica explains the alliances and the Iranian resistance behind the battle.

phases.title: Frontier city
phases.description: Alexandria Eschate is founded; Sogdiana rises and nomad horsemen gather across the river.

phases.title: Engines and crossing
phases.description: Bolt-shooters drive the riders from the bank; archers and slingers screen the landing.

phases.title: Bait and envelopment
phases.description: A forward detachment is surrounded; light infantry and cavalry then attack together and pin the horsemen.

phases.title: Pursuit and terms
phases.description: Alexander's illness cuts the pursuit short; the Scythian king disowns the attack.

perspectives.name: Alexander III of Macedon
perspectives.objective: Secure the river frontier with a decisive defeat of the nomads.
perspectives.known: Horse archers were massed on the far bank, taunting the Macedonians.
perspectives.uncertainty: Whether his landing could survive arrow fire, and whether mounted archers could be made to stand.
perspectives.constraints: He was recovering from a head wound, the sacrifices were unfavourable, and the Sogdian revolt demanded troops in the south.
perspectives.forces: Cavalry, horse-lancers, archers, slingers, Agrianians, the phalanx and bolt-shooting engines.
perspectives.terrain: A river crossing followed by open ground suited to horse archers.
perspectives.logistics: Hide floats for the crossing and the new city as a base.
perspectives.decision: He crossed under the cover of his engines, let a forward detachment draw the horsemen in and attacked with light infantry and cavalry together.
perspectives.outcome: The nomads were routed, but illness cut short the pursuit.

perspectives.name: The Saka (Scythian) horsemen
perspectives.objective: In Arrian's and Livius's accounts, exploit the revolt and defeat the Macedonians as they crossed; Briant describes long-standing alliances between Saka chiefs and the leaders of the revolt.
perspectives.known: The Macedonians were preparing to cross the river.
perspectives.uncertainty: Whether Alexander would risk a crossing against them.
perspectives.constraints: Livius argues that their way of war made them unwilling to sacrifice men to hold ground.
perspectives.forces: Mounted archers.
perspectives.terrain: Open ground on the far bank, suited to wheeling and shooting.
perspectives.logistics: Horses and mobility rather than fixed bases.
perspectives.decision: They harried the river from the bank, pulled back under engine fire and closed on the forward detachment.
perspectives.outcome: Caught between infantry and cavalry, they broke; their king later disowned the attack and, in a letter Plutarch cites, offered Alexander his daughter in marriage.

sources.title: Arrian, Anabasis of Alexander 4.18–19 (trans. E. J. Chinnock)

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: By the winter of 328/327 BCE Spitamenes was dead and Alexander's columns had stormed or garrisoned much of Sogdiana. Alexander wintered at Nautaca. Resistance continued from mountain strongholds.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: Among the refugees on the Sogdian Rock were the wife and daughters of Oxyartes, who had also revolted. Schmitt describes him as a confidant of Bessus who had fled with him across the Oxus and fought on after Bessus's death. Briant explains the revolt's strength: the Bactrian and Sogdian nobles were defending their privileged position and had men, money and arms. Livius describes the campaign as one of forts stormed, populations resettled and countryside ravaged.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Alexander wanted to break the remaining resistance and to secure the families of its leaders, which gave him leverage over them. The defenders trusted that the fortress could outlast a siege.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: Arrian describes a rock steep on every side. Heavy snow made the approach harder for the Macedonians but gave the defenders water, and they had stored provisions for a long siege. Its exact location is unknown.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Many Sogdians had taken refuge on the rock with their families. Chaumont names its commander as Ariamazes and says that Alexander, reaching Nautaca early in 327 BCE, found the whole region prepared for defence and the road ahead guarded by strong fortresses. Alexander had his army and, crucially, soldiers experienced in climbing during sieges.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: Alexander offered the defenders safe passage home if they surrendered. Arrian says they laughed and told him to find soldiers with wings. He then offered graded rewards to the first men to reach the summit.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: Arrian places the advance at the first sign of spring; the notes to the translation and Livius put it in 327 BCE. About three hundred volunteers climbed by night, driving iron tent pegs into bare ground and firm snow and using flax ropes. Arrian says about thirty fell to their deaths. At dawn the survivors signalled from the summit with linen.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: The decisive choices were Alexander's: to send climbers up the steepest and least guarded face rather than settle into a siege, and to send a herald announcing that the winged men had arrived and pointing to the soldiers on the crest.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: Seeing soldiers above them and overestimating their number, the defenders surrendered.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: The captives included the wives and children of many leading men, among them Oxyartes's family. Chaumont says Ariamazes surrendered. Arrian says Alexander married Oxyartes's daughter Roxane rather than treat her as a captive. Livius places the wedding at Bactra in the summer of 327 BCE.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: Livius presents the marriage as a political necessity for pacifying Bactria and Sogdia. It passed over Barsine, mother of Alexander's son Heracles, and slighted her father Artabazus. Schmitt describes the reconciliation that followed: Oxyartes's sons joined the Macedonian army, Oxyartes himself persuaded the lord of another fortress, called Chorienes by Arrian and Sisimithres by Plutarch and Curtius, to surrender, and Alexander later made him satrap of the Paropamisadae, a post he kept after Alexander's death. Chaumont adds that the surrendered lord was reinstated and supplied the army. By the end of the campaign, Livius says, the Bactrian and Sogdian aristocracy had been defeated and the population reduced to serfdom under strong garrisons; Briant stresses the colonists Alexander settled to end the nobility's dominance.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: A small force in an unexpected place can break a defender's will before it breaks his walls. Here coercion was followed by a political settlement through marriage with the local elite whose resistance the campaign had faced, and a former rebel became the instrument for securing the surrender of others.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: The rock's name, location and date are uncertain, and Livius warns that Arrian's narrative of these years is fragmented and contains doublets. Chaumont shows how the sources tangle two sieges: the Rock of the Sogdians, held by Ariamazes, where Roxane was captured, and the rock of Chorienes or Sisimithres, taken through Oxyartes's mediation; Strabo merges them and places the rock in Bactria. Plutarch's story of Alexander asking Oxyartes whether Sisimithres was a coward belongs to the second siege. Arrian calls Oxyartes a Bactrian and Livius a Sogdian nobleman; Schmitt follows Arrian. The notes to the translation say Curtius gives different reward figures from Arrian's. Arrian's romantic framing of the marriage sits beside Livius's reading of it as policy.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: Arrian is the principal narrative. Livius's survey of the Sogdian campaign and his article on Roxane supply the political context and the date and place of the marriage, citing Lucian for its ceremony. The Encyclopaedia Iranica articles by Rüdiger Schmitt on Oxyartes, Marie Louise Chaumont on Chorienes and Pierre Briant on Alexander follow the Iranian leaders and the resistance; Plutarch's Life of Alexander, in the Loeb translation on LacusCurtius, adds the anecdote of Sisimithres.

phases.title: Winter at Nautaca
phases.description: The army rests; Alexander prepares to move against the remaining strongholds.

phases.title: Taunt and reward
phases.description: The defenders reject terms; Alexander offers rewards to volunteer climbers.

phases.title: Night climb
phases.description: About three hundred climbers scale the steepest face with pegs and ropes; some fall to their deaths.

phases.title: Surrender
phases.description: Climbers signal from the summit; the defenders surrender and Oxyartes's family is captured.

perspectives.name: Alexander III of Macedon
perspectives.objective: Take the rock and the families sheltering there without a long siege.
perspectives.known: The rock was steep on all sides, supplied for a long siege and watered by snow.
perspectives.uncertainty: Whether climbers could reach the summit unseen, and whether the defenders would yield when they did.
perspectives.constraints: Snow and cliffs ruled out an ordinary assault, and a blockade could be long.
perspectives.forces: His army, including men experienced in siege climbing.
perspectives.terrain: A snow-covered rock, steep on all sides, with a precipitous face that was less closely guarded.
perspectives.logistics: Iron tent pegs and flax ropes for the climb, and rewards to recruit volunteers.
perspectives.decision: He offered terms, then rewards, sent volunteers up the steepest face by night and announced their arrival by herald.
perspectives.outcome: The garrison surrendered; Oxyartes's family was captured and Alexander married Roxane.

perspectives.name: The Sogdian defenders
perspectives.objective: Outlast the Macedonians on a fortress they believed impregnable.
perspectives.known: Alexander's army was below the rock, offering terms.
perspectives.uncertainty: Whether any part of the rock could be climbed.
perspectives.constraints: They were sheltering families, including Oxyartes's, as well as fighters.
perspectives.forces: Sogdian fighters and refugees under a commander whom Chaumont names as Ariamazes.
perspectives.terrain: A steep rock where the snow gave them water.
perspectives.logistics: Provisions stored for a long siege.
perspectives.decision: They refused terms, taunting Alexander to find soldiers with wings.
perspectives.outcome: Seeing soldiers above them, they surrendered. Oxyartes, whose family was taken, was later reconciled with Alexander and made a satrap.
