sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: In 326 BCE Alexander entered the Punjab. Ambhi of Taxila, whom Arrian calls Taxiles, welcomed him as an ally. Porus, king of the Paurava state between the Hydaspes and the Acesines and Ambhi's enemy, sent no envoys to submit.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: Livius calls Porus's refusal a grave error, since Alexander meant to conquer all of India. Porus held the far bank of the Hydaspes, the modern Jhelum, hoping to gain time with the river between him and the invaders. Diodorus says he had won the support of a neighbouring king, whom he calls Embisarus, and that Alexander decided to attack before this ally arrived.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Porus aimed to stop any crossing at the bank, where his elephants would make horses unwilling to land. Alexander needed a crossing that Porus could not oppose in force; Arrian says he openly gathered grain to suggest he would wait for the river to fall in winter.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: The river was swollen by monsoon rain and Himalayan meltwater. Livius places the battle near modern Jhelum, where the main road to the Ganges plain crossed the river, and suggests a crossing upstream near the modern Mangla dam. Arrian describes a wooded headland at a bend of the river with a wooded island opposite.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Porus had infantry, cavalry, chariots and war elephants. Alexander's striking force combined Companion cavalry, horse archers, the hypaspists, phalanx battalions, archers and Agrianians, while Craterus held the main camp with a large part of the army. Livius calls the battle in fact a skirmish fought with only part of Alexander's army. Arrian's numbers for both sides are not repeated here.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: Porus placed his elephants at intervals in front of his infantry, with further infantry on the wings and cavalry and chariots on each flank, on level, firm ground. Diodorus describes infantry posted between the elephants to protect them from javelins, so that the whole line looked like a city, with the elephants as towers and the men as the walls between them. Alexander massed his cavalry on his right, with horse archers in front and the infantry in order beside it.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: Night after night Alexander's cavalry made noise along the bank as if to cross, until Porus stopped moving his elephants to meet them. In a stormy night Alexander marched to the crossing; at dawn his men crossed in boats and on stuffed hides, landed on what proved to be a large island and forded a deep channel to the far bank. Plutarch, citing Alexander's own letters, describes the storm, the lightning and a breach in the bank that the men waded chest-deep, and says Alexander rode ahead of his infantry, reckoning that his cavalry could beat any horsemen sent against it. They defeated the force sent under Porus's son, then met Porus's main army. Arrian dates the battle to the Athenian month Munychion, Livius to May 326 BCE.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Alexander divided his army: Craterus was to cross only if Porus took all his elephants against Alexander or was beaten, and mercenaries under Meleager, Attalus and Gorgias were to cross in detachments once the Indians were engaged. On the field he declined to attack the elephant line and sent Coenus with two cavalry regiments toward the Indian right, to follow the enemy cavalry if it rode out against him.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: Horse archers and the Companions struck the Indian left. When the Indian cavalry turned to meet Coenus behind them, Alexander charged while they were turning, and they fled to the elephants. In Alexander's letter as Plutarch gives it, Coenus attacked the Indian right directly and both beaten wings fell back on the elephants, where the fighting went on at close quarters until the eighth hour. The phalanx then fought the elephants with javelins aimed at drivers and animals; hemmed in, wounded elephants trampled both sides. Diodorus says Porus gathered the elephants still under control and counter-attacked, until Alexander concentrated his archers and light troops on him; when he collapsed from his wounds, the word spread that he was dead and his army fled.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: Alexander's cavalry encircled the field and the phalanx advanced with locked shields. Craterus crossed and took up the pursuit. Porus's sons and many of his officers were killed. Wounded, Porus withdrew only when his army had broken; brought to Alexander, he asked to be treated as a king, and Alexander restored his kingdom and added territory. Plutarch and Diodorus tell the same story of his restoration, Diodorus explaining it as recognition of his courage, and Plutarch says Alexander gave him the title of satrap.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: Alexander founded Nicaea on the battlefield and Bucephala at the crossing, where his horse Bucephalas died. Diodorus says he also had ships built from the nearby forests, meaning to conquer India and sail down to the Ocean. Soon afterwards the army refused to advance beyond the Hyphasis and Alexander turned back. Porus became a client ruler on the eastern border, keeping that role after Alexander's death until he was murdered in 317 BCE.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: Repeated feints conditioned Porus to ignore a real threat, and dividing the army to cross and concentrating it to fight depended on precise orders, which Arrian preserves for Craterus. Against elephants, cavalry won on the flanks while the infantry absorbed an unfamiliar weapon.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: The crossing and battle sites are disputed; Livius rejects sites farther downstream on palaeohydrological grounds. Arrian reports three versions of the force under Porus's son and prefers Ptolemy's; how far his reliance on Ptolemy, one of Alexander's companions, shapes the account is uncertain. Plutarch's main source is Alexander's own letters, the victor's account, and he sets aside a more dramatic version by Onesicritus. Diodorus omits the river crossing altogether and makes the battle a contest with the elephants and with Porus himself, whom he and Plutarch describe as gigantic; their figures for his height and for the armies are not repeated here. Livius reads the commemorative coinage, which shows Alexander with Zeus's thunderbolt, as a claim that he had brought the rain. His article on Porus calls the king the long-term winner despite his defeat.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: Arrian's chapters are the main narrative and name his own authorities, Ptolemy and Aristobulus. Livius sets them against the terrain and the coinage, and his article on Porus follows the king's later career. Diodorus and Plutarch, in the Loeb translations on LacusCurtius, give the vulgate version of the fighting and the version Plutarch took from Alexander's letters.

phases.title: Feints on the river
phases.description: Alexander gathers grain and stages nightly feints until Porus stops reacting.

phases.title: Crossing in the storm
phases.description: A picked force crosses upstream, lands on an island and fords a deep channel to the far bank.

phases.title: Porus's son
phases.description: The force sent to investigate is defeated; Porus marches against Alexander.

phases.title: Cavalry and elephants
phases.description: Coenus takes the Indian cavalry in the rear; the phalanx fights the elephants and Porus is captured.

perspectives.name: Alexander III of Macedon
perspectives.objective: Cross the Hydaspes and defeat Porus without facing his elephants at the bank.
perspectives.known: Porus guarded the crossing opposite the camp and posted detachments at other fords.
perspectives.uncertainty: Whether Porus would detect the crossing, how he would divide his elephants, and, in Diodorus's account, whether Porus's ally would arrive first.
perspectives.constraints: Horses would not land in the face of elephants, and the river was in flood.
perspectives.forces: Companion cavalry, horse archers, hypaspists, phalanx battalions and light troops, with Craterus holding the main camp.
perspectives.terrain: A swollen river with a wooded headland and islands upstream, and firm ground beyond.
perspectives.logistics: Boats cut apart, carried and reassembled, hides stuffed for floats, and grain gathered as a deception.
perspectives.decision: He wore down Porus's vigilance with feints, crossed upstream in a storm, and attacked the Indian left with cavalry while Coenus rode for the rear.
perspectives.outcome: Porus's army was destroyed and Porus captured; Alexander restored him as a client king.

perspectives.name: Porus, king of the Paurava
perspectives.objective: Hold the river line and prevent a crossing.
perspectives.known: Alexander's army was camped opposite, making noise at night and gathering grain; Diodorus says an allied king was on his way to join him.
perspectives.uncertainty: Which threat was real, and whether Craterus's force would also cross.
perspectives.constraints: He had to watch many fords and keep part of his army facing Craterus.
perspectives.forces: Infantry, cavalry, chariots and war elephants.
perspectives.terrain: Level, firm ground that he chose for his battle line once Alexander had crossed.
perspectives.logistics: Arrian notes that the clayey ground made his son's chariots slow.
perspectives.decision: He stopped reacting to the feints, sent his son to investigate, then marched against Alexander, leaving some elephants facing Craterus, and drew up his elephants with infantry between them.
perspectives.outcome: His army was broken; wounded, he surrendered and was confirmed as king under Alexander, in recognition of his courage according to Diodorus.

sources.title: Arrian, Anabasis of Alexander 6.4–13 (trans. E. J. Chinnock)
Diodorus Siculus, Library of History 17.98–99 (Loeb translation)

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: After the army refused to go beyond the Hyphasis, Alexander turned south and in November 326 BCE began the voyage down the rivers toward the Indus and the sea. Arrian says he learned that the Mallians and the Oxydracians, the most numerous and warlike peoples of the region, had put their women and children into their strongest cities and meant to fight, and he hurried on to attack them before they were ready. Lendering places the fighting in January 325 and the Mallians near modern Multan.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: Diodorus says the two peoples had been at war with each other, made peace as Alexander approached, and then quarrelled over the command and withdrew into their cities. Arrian calls the Mallians an independent people. Lendering notes that the populous river valleys of Egypt and Babylonia had not resisted the Macedonians, while the peoples along the Indus did, and he judges the war against them merciless.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Alexander divided his forces so that the Mallians could neither unite nor escape. Arrian says the fleet under Nearchus went ahead down the river, Hephaestion marched five days in advance to catch anyone fleeing before the main force, Ptolemy followed three days behind to catch anyone turning back, and all were to meet at the confluence of the Acesines and the Hydraotes. Alexander himself took a picked force across waterless country to fall on the Mallian towns from an unexpected direction.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: The approach crossed a tract without water, covered in a day and a night of marching. The Mallian towns lay near the Hydraotes, with woods along its banks where fugitives hid. The town where Alexander was wounded had walls of earth and a citadel with towers; Arrian mentions a mound of earth inside, close to the wall, from which defenders could throw at him. Lendering identifies the Mallian capital with Multan, a modern identification the ancient narratives do not make.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Alexander led the shield-bearing guards, the archers, the Agrianians, Peithon's brigade of foot Companions, the horse archers and half the Companion cavalry, with Perdiccas commanding a second column. The Mallians defended their towns and, at the Hydraotes, formed a dense array against his cavalry; neither Arrian nor Diodorus names a Mallian commander. Arrian and Diodorus give large figures for the Indian forces, which are not repeated here.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: Alexander's night march caught many Mallians outside their first town and unarmed, Arrian says, because they did not believe he would come through the waterless country; he used his cavalry as a ring round the walls until the infantry arrived, and the citadel was stormed. He then pursued the Mallians across the Hydraotes. When they drew up on the far bank and saw he had only cavalry, they turned and fought, until his light infantry and phalanx came up; they then fled into the strongest of their nearby cities, and Alexander camped round it for the night.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: The next day the army attacked in two divisions, one under Alexander and one under Perdiccas. The defenders abandoned the town walls for the citadel. Alexander's men broke in through a small gate; Perdiccas's men were late, having brought no ladders. At the citadel Alexander, thinking the ladder-bearers too slow, seized a ladder, climbed it under his shield and cleared the battlement. Peucestas, carrying the sacred shield from the temple of Athena at Troy, followed him, with Leonnatus, and Abreas on another ladder. The shield-bearing guards, rushing to follow the king, broke the ladder.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Standing alone on the wall under missiles from the towers, Alexander leapt down into the citadel. Arrian gives his reasoning: if he stayed where he was he would be in danger to no purpose, but if he jumped down he might terrify the defenders, and if not, he would at least die after deeds worth remembering. Diodorus adds that a seer, Demophon, had warned him of a great danger from a wound in this assault and begged him to leave the city alone, and that Alexander rebuked him for discouraging the soldiers.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: Inside, with his back to the wall, Alexander killed the defenders' leader and others who came at him. Abreas was killed by an arrow in the forehead. An arrow went through Alexander's breastplate into his chest, and Ptolemy, Arrian says, reports that air came out of the wound with the blood. He fought until he fainted and fell on his shield, with Peucestas and Leonnatus, both wounded, standing over him. Outside, the Macedonians climbed the earth wall on pegs and on each other's shoulders, and others broke the bar of a gate and forced it open.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: Arrian says the Macedonians, believing their king dead or dying, killed everyone in the citadel and spared neither women nor children; Diodorus says that in their fury they filled the city with corpses. Alexander was carried out on his shield. Some writers, Arrian says, had Critodemus, a physician of Cos, cut out the arrow; others say Perdiccas did it with his sword at Alexander's bidding. The loss of blood made him faint again, and the bleeding stopped. Plutarch says the arrowhead was lodged in a rib and that its removal brought him close to death.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: Diodorus says that the false report of Alexander's death led Greek settlers in Bactria and Sogdiana to revolt and march for home. For fear of unrest in his own army, Arrian says, Alexander had himself carried to the river as soon as it was safe and taken by boat to the camp at the confluence of the Hydraotes and the Acesines. Lendering says the last Mallians surrendered, followed by the Oxydracae; Alexander made the region a satrapy under Peithon and Oxyartes and founded an Alexandria near the confluence of the Indus and the Acesines.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: Alexander's habit of leading assaults in person drove his men to follow him, and it was their rush up the ladder that left him alone on the wall. The same bond made his wound a danger to the whole army: Plutarch says the camp believed him dead, and Arrian that he feared unrest in the army. The citadel he took at that risk was a minor objective, and its people paid for his wound.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: Arrian complains that the common account placed this disaster among the Oxydracians, not the Mallians, and that some writers made Ptolemy one of the king's rescuers, though Ptolemy himself recorded that he was elsewhere. The rescuers differ: Arrian names Peucestas, Leonnatus and Abreas, Plutarch Peucestas and Limnaeus, and Diodorus Peucestas. Some writers, Arrian notes, said Alexander was first struck on the head; Plutarch has a blow on the neck with a club. Diodorus sets the episode at the first city attacked and has Alexander shelter by a tree, while Arrian puts it at the strongest city, after the crossing of the Hydraotes. The identification with Multan is modern.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: Arrian gives the campaign, the assault and the wound in most detail, from Ptolemy, and corrects other writers by name. Diodorus, from the vulgate, adds the seer and the revolt of the settlers. Plutarch gives the wound and its treatment. Lendering's survey dates the campaign and places it in the descent of the Indus.

phases.title: Across the desert
phases.description: A night march across waterless country surprises the first Mallian town; its citadel is stormed.

phases.title: The Hydraotes
phases.description: Alexander forces the river with his cavalry and drives the Mallians into their strongest city.

phases.title: The ladder
phases.description: The town falls; at the citadel Alexander climbs alone, the ladder breaks and he leaps inside.

phases.title: The wound
phases.description: Alexander is shot through the chest; his men break in and kill the defenders, and he is carried out barely alive.

perspectives.name: Alexander III of Macedon
perspectives.objective: Defeat the Mallians before they could join the Oxydracians and secure the descent of the rivers.
perspectives.known: The Mallians had gathered in their strongest towns, and his columns were placed to catch any who fled.
perspectives.uncertainty: Where the Mallians would stand and how long their citadels would hold.
perspectives.constraints: His picked force had outmarched its infantry, and the ladders were too few and too slow.
perspectives.forces: Shield-bearing guards, archers, Agrianians, foot Companions, horse archers and half the Companion cavalry.
perspectives.terrain: Waterless country, the Hydraotes and its wooded banks, and towns with earth walls and towered citadels.
perspectives.logistics: His men filled their vessels at the last water before the desert and marched through the night.
perspectives.decision: He climbed the citadel wall himself and, left alone when the ladder broke, leapt down inside.
perspectives.outcome: The citadel fell and its people were killed; he was so badly wounded that the army believed him dead.

perspectives.name: The Mallian defenders
perspectives.objective: Defend their towns and families against the invasion.
perspectives.known: Alexander was coming down the rivers; they had put their women and children in their strongest cities.
perspectives.uncertainty: Whether the Oxydracians would fight beside them, and from which direction the attack would come.
perspectives.constraints: Diodorus says their alliance broke down in a dispute over the command before the attack.
perspectives.forces: Town garrisons and a field army that stood against Alexander's cavalry at the Hydraotes.
perspectives.terrain: Earth-walled towns with citadels, a river line and woods along its banks.
perspectives.logistics: They believed no army could cross the waterless country to reach them.
perspectives.decision: They abandoned their outer walls and held the citadel, where they nearly killed Alexander.
perspectives.outcome: The citadel was stormed and its people killed; the last Mallians later surrendered.
